## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Advanced Topics in Large Language Models
  Code                    M2 · P2 (announced) — official code not published (course description not published)
  Team and workload       Instructor: master's team · \~24 h · research seminar: reasoning (CoT, RLVR), long context, memory, MoE, alternative architectures (Mamba), efficiency, the LLMs × graphs crossroads, agents, evaluation, open problems — each chapter organizes the critical reading of a pivot paper.
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2}[Outside the recommended track]{.badge .position} · M2 program being finalized
  ----------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer / researcher who already reads LLM papers and wants a critical filter. **Empirical first**: "magic" CoT that drops out of distribution; 1M-token long context lost in the middle — then we name RLVR, MoE, Mamba, agents, eval contamination.

Reading seminar: reasoning, memory, architectures, efficiency, evaluation.

### What you will be able to do

-   Read an LLM research paper critically: claims, evidence, protocol, what the authors do not say;
-   Explain model reasoning: chain-of-thought, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR);
-   Analyze long-context techniques (RoPE, ring attention) and arbitrate between long context and RAG;
-   Compare agent memories: episodic, vector stores, GraphRAG;
-   Explain how mixture-of-experts architectures and alternatives to transformers (SSM, Mamba, RWKV) work and why they matter;
-   Speed up inference with speculative decoding and quantization, quantifying the trade-offs;
-   Analyze the LLMs × graphs crossroads and agent architectures (planning, tools, multi-agents);
-   Evaluate an LLM without deceiving oneself: benchmark contamination, LLM judge bias, open problems.

### Where this course fits in the program

An M2 module offered in period 2, outside the recommended track: a research seminar, it assumes the foundations are laid and works through readings and discussions rather than ex cathedra lectures. **Prerequisites**: [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) (architecture, training, alignment — the foundation that every chapter goes beyond) and [Advanced Deep Learning](../m1p2-advanced-deep-learning/index.html), whose architectures and efficiency analyses are reused continuously.

**Downstream**: it is the direct preparation for the research internship and the PhD — each chapter ends with open questions that are as many internship topics — and for R&D jobs, where the competitive edge is played on a six-month head start in reading the literature.

### Course outline

-   **Recap and how to use the seminar** — the LLM foundation recapped, and the method: how one reads, discusses and presents a paper here.
-   **Reasoning: chain-of-thought, RLVR** — have the model unfold a reasoning, then train it on verifiable rewards.
-   **Long context: RoPE, ring attention, RAG or LC?** — extend the window, and the real industrial question: put everything in context or retrieve?
-   **Memory: episodic, vector stores, GraphRAG** — give memory beyond the window, from vector storage to knowledge graphs.
-   **Mixture-of-Experts** — immense models of which only a few experts activate: training, routing, savings.
-   **Alternative architectures: SSM, Mamba, RWKV** — thinking beyond attention: promises and measured realities.
-   **Efficiency: speculative decoding, quantization** — serve faster and cheaper, with their effects on quality.
-   **LLMs × graphs: the LLGA crossroads** — reasoning on structures, GraphRAG, graph foundation models: the master's signature.
-   **Agents: planning, tools, multi-agents** — models that plan, call tools and collaborate.
-   **Evaluation: contamination, judge bias** — why leaderboards are wrong, and how to evaluate honestly.
-   **Open problems** — the map of research fronts as it takes shape this year.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — minimal reproductions: RoPE, speculative decoding, a small contamination-free evaluation.
-   **References** — the pivot papers of each chapter, with their rebuttals.

### How to study this module

-   Read each paper *before* the session, in a first twenty-minute pass (abstract, figures, protocol), then a second targeted pass: the seminar only works if everyone has read.
-   For each paper, write down the sentence "the central claim is X, proven by Y, fragile because Z": it is the module's single exercise, do it every week.
-   Present at the board when it is your turn: explaining RoPE or speculative decoding without slides is the best rehearsal for a PhD interview.
-   Systematically cross with the other modules: long context dialogues with the RAG Ops of ML Ops, agents with Speech Technology, ch. 7 with your graph courses.
-   Follow two or three preprint sources after each chapter: the module above all teaches you to stay up to date by yourself.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} Chapter 7 is called "LLMs × graphs: the LLGA crossroads": this module is the place in the master where the motto becomes a research object. The fronts it covers — reasoning, memory, agents, evaluation — are exactly those where the crossroads of language models with relational data produces the most open questions. If you are aiming for a PhD, an R&D internship or a startup at the frontier, this is where you will learn the rarest gesture: read fast, judge surely, and identify the problem that no one has yet posed well.
:::

::: note
[Independent note]{.tag} Reading filter for the 2-year path: protocols and failure modes before slogans.
:::

## 1. Reasoning: chain-of-thought, RLVR {#ch1}

Concrete scene: a SOTA benchmark… contaminated by the train set. This chapter organizes CoT / reasoning reading.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Reading the abstract without the protocol; confusing context length with real use; a contaminated score taken as capability.
:::

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} J. Wei et al., *Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models*, NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2201.11903); X. Wang et al., *Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models*, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2203.11171); H. Lightman et al., *Let's Verify Step by Step*, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2305.20050); DeepSeek-AI, *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning*, 2025 (arXiv:2501.12948); N. Lambert et al., *Tulu 3*, 2024 (arXiv:2411.15124) — which names RLVR (*reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards*).
:::

### 1.1. Chain-of-thought and self-consistency

The prompt "let's think step by step" triggers the generation of an intermediate reasoning chain $z$ before the answer $y$ — and the gains *emerge* with scale (clear from \~10^11^ parameters in the original study): the model allocates compute tokens to the problem. The formal reading:

::: prop
[Proposition 1.1 — Self-consistency = marginalization (Wang et al., 2023)]{.tag} Generating a chain $z$ then an answer $y$ realizes a joint model $p(y, z \mid x) = p(z\mid x)\,p(y \mid x, z)$. The probability of the correct answer under the full model is the *margin* $$p(y \mid x) \;=\; \sum_{z} p(y, z \mid x).$$ Self-consistency approximates $\arg\max_y p(y\mid x)$ by majority vote over $k$ sampled chains $z_1, \dots, z_k \sim p(\cdot \mid x)$: a Monte Carlo of "latent reasoning". Typical gains: +10 to +20 points on GSM8K compared to greedy decoding — for an inference cost of ×$k$.
:::

::: proof
Sampling $z_i \sim p(z\mid x)$ then $y_i \sim p(y \mid x, z_i)$ produces pairs $(y_i, z_i)$ distributed according to the joint; the count $\frac1k \sum_i \mathbf{1}[y_i = y]$ is an unbiased estimator of $\sum_z p(z \mid x)\,p(y \mid x, z) = p(y\mid x)$ (the two successive samplings compose exactly the joint). The empirical argmax converges to the true argmax as $k \to \infty$ (concentration of frequencies) — it is a special case of the Monte Carlo marginalization seen in the ML module, with the particularity that the latent space is *text*. [∎]{.qed}
:::

### 1.2. Process vs outcome rewards

Training a reward model on the final answer (**ORM**, outcome) is noisy: an answer that is right by chance receives the same reward as a clean reasoning. Lightman et al. build PRM800K (800,000 *step-by-step* labels given by humans) and train a **PRM** (process reward model): at equal labeling budget, the PRM selects better solutions on MATH than the ORM — supervision *of the process* is more informative than that of the outcome. Immediate limit: step-by-step labeling is expensive and subjective; hence the idea of automating verification...

### 1.3. RLVR: verifiable rewards and the emergence of reasoning

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — RLVR]{.tag} Instead of a learned reward model (subject to *reward hacking*), the reward is a **verifiable rule**: does the mathematical answer match the ground truth? does the code pass the tests? is the format correct? Training (GRPO — cf. LLMs module ch. 5; PPO — cf. RL module ch. 4) maximizes $$\mathcal{J}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(x, y)\sim \pi_\theta} \bigl[\, r_{\text{verif}}(x, y) \,\bigr]$$ over domains where truth is *decidable*. Tulu 3 (Lambert et al., 2024) makes it the third stage of open post-training (SFT → DPO → RLVR).
:::

::: ex
[Pivot result — DeepSeek-R1 (2025)]{.tag} R1-Zero: *purely* RL (no initial SFT) with rule-based rewards on math/code/format; the model **develops by itself** reasoning behaviors — verification, backtracking, reflection ("aha moment"), lengthening chains — measurable by the growing generation length over the course of training. R1: adding cold-start data + multiple stages (SFT → RL → re-SFT) stabilizes and aligns, up to rivaling the best closed reasoning models on math/code benchmarks. Associated publication in *Nature* (2025) — read both: the technical account and the scientific letter do not tell exactly the same story.
:::

::: note
[Critical analysis (a whole session)]{.tag} (i) *Generalization*: RLVR only improves domains close to pre-training + verifiable; transfer to "general" reasoning is debated. (ii) *Benchmarks*: MATH/AIME are saturated and contaminable (ch. 9); are the advances measured on the scale of their own pollution? (iii) *Residual reward hacking*: even "hard" rules are bypassable (misleading format, weak tests); (iv) *Costs*: chains of tens of thousands of tokens — reasoning is a product that is *compute-bound at inference* (cf. ML Ops module ch. 4, green ops ch. 10); (v) *Alternative reading*: does R1-Zero *select* capabilities already present (pre-training) rather than *create* them? The distillation experiments (small models trained on R1's traces outperforming their direct RL cousins) lean toward the first reading. Exercise: defend both theses with the figures of the paper.
:::

## 2. Long context: RoPE, ring attention, RAG or LC? {#ch2}

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} J. Su et al., *RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding* (RoPE), 2021 (arXiv:2104.09864); S. Chen et al., *Extending Context Window via Positional Interpolation*, 2023 (arXiv:2306.15595); B. Peng et al., *YaRN*, 2023 (arXiv:2309.00071); H. Liu et al., *Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context*, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2310.01889); N. Liu et al., *Lost in the Middle*, 2023 (arXiv:2307.03172); Z. Li et al., *Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs?*, EMNLP 2024 industry (arXiv:2407.16833); P. Xu et al., *Retrieval meets Long Context LLMs*, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.03025).
:::

### 2.1. RoPE: position by rotation

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — RoPE (Su et al., 2021)]{.tag} Each even coordinate pair $(2i, 2i{+}1)$ of the vector is viewed as a complex number to which a rotation of angle $m\theta_i$ is applied, with $m$ the position of the token and $\theta_i = b^{-2i/d}$ (geometric bases): $$q_m = R(m\Theta)\, q, \qquad k_n = R(n\Theta)\, k, \qquad \Theta = \mathrm{diag}(\theta_0, \dots).$$ The attention dot product becomes a function *of the relative position* — and the high frequencies $\theta_i$ resolve the local, the low frequencies the global.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — RoPE encodes only relative position]{.tag} $\langle R(m\Theta)\,q,\; R(n\Theta)\,k \rangle$ depends only on $m - n$ (and on $q, k$). The proof is one line of trigonometry: per coordinate pairs, $$\langle R(m\theta)q,\, R(n\theta)k\rangle = \langle R((m-n)\theta)\, q,\; k \rangle,$$ since $R(m\theta)^\top R(n\theta) = R((n-m)\theta)$ (composition of the rotations — they commute in the plane).
:::

::: proof
Plane rotations are orthogonal: $\langle R(m\theta)q, R(n\theta)k\rangle = q^\top R(m\theta)^\top R(n\theta)k = q^\top R((n - m)\theta)k$. Summing over the coordinate pairs (each pair with its own frequency $\theta_i$), the attention score is a function of $m - n$ only. Engineering consequence: extending the context amounts to *re-parameterizing the angles*, not to relearning positional embeddings. [∎]{.qed}
:::

### 2.2. Extending the window: interpolation and YaRN

**Positional interpolation** (Chen et al., 2023): trained with angles up to $L$, one serves $L' > L$ by linearly compressing the positions $m \mapsto m \cdot L/L'$ — the model sees angles already covered; a few hundred fine-tuning steps suffice (Llama-2 4k → 32k). **YaRN** (Peng et al., 2023) refines: interpolate *selectively* by frequency (the low — global — frequencies are interpolated; the high — local — extrapolated; "NTK-aware") and **rescale the attention temperature** ($\times$ constant depending on the extension factor) to compensate for the dilution of the scores; result: an extension that reduces data and fine-tuning steps by roughly 10× compared to PI. Spectral viewpoint (cf. Signal Processing module): handling a larger window = handling a wider frequency spectrum without aliasing.

### 2.3. Ring attention: cutting the memory cost in a ring

::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Ring Attention (Liu et al., NeurIPS 2023)]{.tag} Cut the sequence of length $N$ into $D$ blocks distributed over $D$ GPUs; at each step, each GPU computes the attention of its query block *against a key/value block* received from a neighbor, then passes this block to the next (ring topology) — *overlapping communication and computation*. After $D$ steps, each query has seen *all* the blocks: the attention is **exact** (not an approximation), and the memory *per GPU* drops from $\mathcal{O}(N)$ to $\mathcal{O}(N/D)$. Demonstration at scale: contexts on the order of 32 million tokens on 32 A100 GPUs — \~27× the memory state of the art of the time.
:::

### 2.4. RAG or long context? Lost in the middle and the hybrid router

"Lost in the Middle" (N. Liu et al., 2023): when the information is placed in the *middle* of a long context, performance collapses in a U shape (beginning and end favored) — a 128k window does not "read" its 128k uniformly. The RAG vs LC dossier: Li et al. (2024) compare systematically on long-context tasks: with sufficient resources, **long context wins on average** (retrieval can miss the needle); but RAG remains *much* more economical — and their **Self-Route** (the model estimates whether the query is answerable with the retrieved excerpts; if not, the whole document is sent) achieves LC quality for \~39% less cost. Xu et al. (ICLR 2024) complete the picture: retrieval *improves* models whatever the window (4k/16k/32k), and a 4k + retrieval approaches a 16k without retrieval — RAG is not dead, it is *complementary*.

::: note
[Critical analysis]{.tag} (i) "Needle in a haystack" (finding a sentence planted in a long text) is a *retrieval* test, not a long-context reasoning test — multi-document aggregation benchmarks break the scoreboard; (ii) the KV cache grows linearly with $N$ (cf. ML Ops module ch. 3): "free" LC at the API is an *economic choice* of the provider, not a physical property; (iii) RoPE extensions are measured in perplexity *and* in downstream tasks — YaRN shows they can diverge; (iv) Self-Route relies on the model's self-assessment (meta-cognition): how good is it on adversarial queries? To be related to ch. 3 (memory) and the ML Ops module ch. 6 (index cost vs context cost).
:::

```python
# Self-Route self-evaluation (sketch) -- RAG first, LC as fallback
def self_route(question, docs, llm, budget):
    snippets = retrieve(question, docs, k=8)          # classic RAG
    verdict = llm(f"Sauras-tu repondre avec SEULEMENT ces extraits ? "
                  f"(OUI/NON)\n---\n{snippets}", max_tokens=2, temp=0)
    if verdict.strip().upper().startswith("OUI"):
        return llm(f"Extraits :\n{snippets}\nQuestion : {question}")
    return llm(f"Documents complets :\n{concat(docs)}\nQuestion : {question}")
    # cost: ~39% of full LC if the router is well calibrated (Li et al. 2024)
```

## 3. Memory: episodic, vector stores, GraphRAG {#ch3}

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} Y. Wu et al., *Memorizing Transformers*, ICLR 2022 (arXiv:2203.08913); J. Park et al., *Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior*, UIST 2023 (arXiv:2304.03442); C. Packer et al., *MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems*, 2023 (arXiv:2310.08560); D. Edge et al., *From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach*, 2024 (arXiv:2404.16130).
:::

### 3.1. A taxonomy of memories

  Type                Cognitive analogue   Implementation                                       Example (paper)
  ------------------- -------------------- ---------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------
  Context             working memory       KV window                                            — (cf. ch. 2 here, LLMs ch. 2)
  Episodic            event memories       journal + retrieval (recency/importance/relevance)   Generative Agents (2023)
  External semantic   knowledge            vector store / index (RAG)                           LLMs ch. 7, ML Ops ch. 6
  Structured          —                    entity graph + summaries                             GraphRAG (2024)
  Paged               —                    context + external storage managed by the model      MemGPT (2023)

### 3.2. Three papers, three ideas of memory

-   **Memorizing Transformers (Wu et al., 2022)**: an attention layer, *non-differentiable*, looks up its keys/values in an external memory of $(k, v)$ pairs by nearest neighbors (kNN) over *past* tokens — including other documents. The model learns to *use* a raw memory; effective for perplexity, but the memory is frozen (no update during generation).
-   **Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023)**: 25 simulated agents in a virtual small town; each agent owns a timestamped *memory stream*; retrieval weights **recency × importance × relevance**; a **reflection** process periodically synthesizes the memories into higher-level beliefs ("I should organize a party"), re-injected as memories. The conceptual architecture of every memory-equipped conversational agent.
-   **MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023)**: the model becomes its own *operating system*: main context (RAM) vs external storage (disk), paging driven by function calls the LLM triggers itself (`core_memory_append`, `archival_memory_insert`…). Memory management becomes a *learned/instructed behavior* — the ancestor of the "agent + notepad" loops.
-   **GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024)**: *structured* memory — an entity graph extracted by an LLM, communities detected (Leiden), hierarchical summaries; global questions ("which themes?") become a map-reduce over the community summaries, where vector RAG falls apart (cf. Graph ML module ch. 11 for the graph foundations; ML Ops module ch. 6 for the indexing cost).

::: prop
[Proposition 3.1 — The retrieval triptych of generative agents]{.tag} The retrieval score of a memory $s$ at time $t$ for the query $q$ reads $$\mathrm{score}(s; q, t) \;=\; w_r\, e^{-\Delta t/\tau} \;+\; w_i\, \mathrm{imp}(s) \;+\; w_p\, \cos\bigl(e(s), e(q)\bigr),$$ exponential recency + importance (predicted by the LLM at writing time) + semantic relevance. This is exactly the signal fusion of a search engine reranker (cf. NLP ch. 2): "agent memory" reinvents *learning to rank* — the originality lies in the **reflection** loop that creates new synthetic memories.
:::

::: note
[Critical analysis]{.tag} (i) *Evaluation*: each of these papers evaluates memory differently (perplexity, simulated interviews, multi-session dialogues, global questions) — no consensus benchmark; wariness toward small-sample gains. (ii) *Writing*: the hard question is *what one stores* (everything? a summary? a graph?) and *when one forgets*; MemGPT delegates to the model, GraphRAG to a pipeline — two philosophies (agency vs infrastructure). (iii) *Context fraud*: with windows of a million tokens (ch. 2), "keep everything in the context" becomes credible again — until the next "lost in the middle". (iv) *LLGA position*: graph-structured memory is the exact place where the master crosses its two legs (LLMs + graphs); ch. 7 comes back to it.
:::

## 4. Mixture-of-Experts {#ch4}

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} N. Shazeer et al., *Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer*, ICLR 2017 (arXiv:1701.06538); W. Fedus, B. Zoph, N. Shazeer, *Switch Transformers*, JMLR 2022 (arXiv:2101.03961); A. Jiang et al., *Mixtral of Experts*, 2024 (arXiv:2401.04088); DeepSeek-AI, *DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report*, 2024 (arXiv:2412.19437).
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Sparse MoE layer]{.tag} Each feed-forward block is replaced by $N$ experts $E_1, \dots, E_N$ and a router: $$y \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathrm{TopK}(g(x))} g_i(x)\, E_i(x), \qquad g(x) = \mathrm{softmax}\bigl(W_g\,x\bigr),$$ only the $k$ strongest experts are computed (k = 1-2 typically). The *total* parameters grow (capacity), the *active parameters per token* remain bounded (cost): Mixtral 8×7B = \~47B parameters, \~13B active; DeepSeek-V3 = 671B of which \~37B active.
:::

### 4.1. Balancing the experts: the auxiliary loss

::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Auxiliary load-balancing loss (Switch)]{.tag} With $f_i$ = fraction of tokens *routed* to expert $i$ and $P_i$ = *average* router probability mass on $i$: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} \;=\; \alpha\, N \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i\, P_i, \qquad \sum_i f_i = \sum_i P_i = 1,$$ whose minimum $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha$ is reached at uniform routing $f = P = \mathbf{1}/N$. The loss penalizes the degenerate routing where a few experts capture everything — otherwise the router gradient collapses (the unpicked experts receive no gradient: the rich get richer).
:::

::: proof
At the uniform point, $\sum_i f_iP_i = N \cdot \frac1N \cdot \frac1N = \frac1N$, so $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha N \cdot \frac1N = \alpha$. To show that this is indeed a *minimum in the targeted regime*, we use Chebyshev's sum inequality: if the sequences $(f_i)$ and $(P_i)$ are *similarly ordered* (co-monotone — the likely experts are also the most loaded, exactly the degenerate regime that we want to penalize), then $$\frac1N \sum_i f_i P_i \;\geq\; \Bigl(\frac1N \sum_i f_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac1N \sum_i P_i\Bigr) = \frac{1}{N^2}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \sum_i f_i P_i \;\geq\; \frac1N,$$ with equality if and only if one of the sequences is constant. Hence $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} \geq \alpha$, equality at uniform. Finally, the dynamic effect: $\partial (f_iP_i)/\partial P_i = f_i \geq 0$ — the gradient pulls $P_i$ down *proportionally to the load* $f_i$: a negative feedback loop against concentration. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Critical analysis — read the hidden assumption]{.tag} The lower bound is only *proved* for co-monotone $(f, P)$: an anti-monotone pair (a very likely but lightly loaded expert) could have a product *below* $1/N$ — the loss is not a symmetric divergence in the strict sense; it is a *load proxy* whose gradient dynamics does most of the work. This is exactly the kind of detail a critical paper reading must catch: what quantity does the loss *actually* measure, under what assumption, and what does its gradient do? DeepSeek-V3 goes as far as replacing the loop with **auxiliary-loss-free balancing**: a per-expert bias term, dynamically adjusted to the observed load — direct control rather than a differentiable penalty, with reported quality gains. Less elegant, more effective: up for debate.
:::

### 4.2. What the experts learn

The Mixtral analysis (the "routing" figure) shows *syntactic and domain-level* specialization (code, math, languages) rather than fine-grained topics — and substantial redundancy across experts: the MoE mostly democratizes **capacity**, not the division of labor. DeepSeek-V3 pushes two structural innovations: *fine-grained* experts (more numerous, smaller) + **shared experts** (always active, capturing cross-cutting knowledge — reducing the redundancy), and FP8 training at scale (14.8T tokens) — the technical report is a systems-engineering course in itself (expert-parallel communication, cf. Emerging ML module ch. 2 on distributed computing).

::: note
[Critique in practice — what are the "active parameters" for?]{.tag} Comparing a 47B/13B-active MoE to a 13B dense model is misleading: the MoE keeps 47B in memory (cf. ML Ops module ch. 3: the KV cache and the weights reside in full in VRAM) but \~13B of compute per token. MoE wins *provided* large batches (amortizing memory through throughput): excellent for shared serving, debatable for single-user. The LLGA reading grid: every architecture must be evaluated at *full cost* (memory, compute, communication) — not in advertising "parameters".
:::

## 5. Alternative architectures: SSM, Mamba, RWKV {#ch5}

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} A. Gu, K. Goel, C. Ré, *Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces* (S4), ICLR 2022 (arXiv:2111.00396); A. Gu & T. Dao, *Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces*, 2023 (arXiv:2312.00752); B. Peng et al., *RWKV: Reinventing RNNs for the Transformer Era*, Findings of EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.13048); S. De et al., *Griffin: RecurrentGating Linear Networks* (Hawk / Griffin), ICML 2024 (arXiv:2402.19427); AI21, *Jamba: A Hybrid Transformer-Mamba Language Model*, 2024 (arXiv:2403.19887).
:::

### 5.1. From RNNs to state space models

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Discrete SSM]{.tag} A state space model maps the input $u_t$ to the output $y_t$ via a linear hidden state $x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$: $$x_{t} = \bar A\, x_{t-1} + \bar B\, u_t, \qquad y_t = C\, x_t,$$ where $(\bar A, \bar B)$ come from the (zero-order) discretization of the continuous system $\dot x = A x + B u$ with step $\Delta$: $\bar A = \exp(\Delta A)$, $\bar B = (\Delta A)^{-1}\bigl(\exp(\Delta A) - I\bigr)\,\Delta B$. The classic RNN reappears with a *structured* state matrix (S4: diagonal + low-rank terms, inherited from HiPPO to memorize the long history).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — LTI ⇒ convolution (S4)]{.tag} If $(\bar A, \bar B, C)$ are *constant* (independent of time and input — LTI), then the system is a convolution product: $$y_t = \sum_{s=0}^{t} \overline{K}_s\, u_{t-s}, \qquad \overline{K} = \bigl(C\bar B,\; C\bar A \bar B,\; C\bar A^2 \bar B,\; \dots\bigr),$$ computable in $\mathcal{O}(L \log L)$ via FFT (Signal Processing module): parallel training over the whole sequence, like a transformer.
:::

::: proof
Let us unroll the recurrence from $x_{-1} = 0$ (zero initial state): $x_0 = \bar B u_0$; $x_1 = \bar A \bar B u_0 + \bar B u_1$; by immediate induction, $x_t = \sum_{s=0}^{t} \bar A^{\,t-s}\, \bar B\, u_s$. Then $y_t = C x_t = \sum_{s=0}^{t} (C \bar A^{\,t-s} \bar B)\, u_s = \sum_{s=0}^{t} \overline K_{t-s}\, u_s$ — a discrete convolution with kernel $\overline K_s = C \bar A^s \bar B$, where the structure of $\bar A$ (diagonal) makes each term computable in $\mathcal{O}(d)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

### 5.2. Mamba: making the state *selective*

The LTI SSM is a *fixed filter*: it cannot choose to memorize or forget depending on the content. **Mamba** (Gu & Dao, 2023) makes $\Delta_t, \bar B_t, C_t$ *functions of the input* (small MLPs on $u_t$): the selection. Cascade consequence: the convolution (prop. 5.2) is destroyed (the kernel depends on position) → back to a recurrence, but *parallelizable* via the **prefix scan** (associativity of $(\bar A_t, \bar B_t)$ — Blelloch's algorithm; cf. Refresher CS) with fused GPU kernels ("hardware-aware"): $\mathcal{O}(L)$ training, $\mathcal{O}(1)$ inference per token and *constant* state memory — the selling point against the transformer's KV cache (cf. ML Ops module ch. 3). Finally, Mamba embeds the SSM *inside* a *gated* MLP-style block. Mamba-2 (SSD) will reformulate the SSM × linear attention duality — the loop comes full circle with ch. 6.

### 5.3. RWKV and the hybrids

::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — RWKV: linearizing attention into an RNN (Peng et al., 2023)]{.tag} RWKV rewrites attention as a recurrence with *per-channel* decay (time-mixing): $$w_t = \sigma(W_t)\odot w_{t-1} + k_t, \qquad y_t = r_t \odot \frac{v_t}{w_t + \epsilon},$$ (schematic form): the state $w_t$ accumulates past values channel-wise with a learned exponential decay ($r_t$ = *receptance*, $v_t$ the step's value) — a linear attention *normalized over time*, trainable in parallel (like a transformer), executable as an RNN (constant memory). At scale: models up to 14B — the largest RNNs ever trained at its publication.
:::

**Hybrids**: pure SSMs lose on **exact recall** tasks (copying an association seen a long time ago: the compressed state has no room to keep everything — a recurring critique, cf. the associative recall studies); hence mixed architectures: Jamba (AI21, 2024) interleaves attention + Mamba + MoE blocks (1:7:1) and shows that \~one attention layer in eight suffices to restore recall; Griffin/De et al. (2024) alternate recurrence (RG-LRU) and local attention. The 2024-2026 consensus: *attention is irreplaceable for precise retrieval; the SSM excels at long context on a constant memory budget; the hybrid beats both*.

::: note
[Critical analysis]{.tag} (i) The "Mamba matches transformers at X times less memory" curves are established *at calibrated data and compute sizes*; transformers have an ecosystem (serving, quantization, ch. 6) that SSMs lack — the real adoption cost exceeds the paper. (ii) Exact recall is a *limit case* (one key among millions): needle-in-a-haystack-style benchmarks are highly sensitive to it, comprehension tasks far less so. (iii) RWKV illustrates the virtue of deployable simplicity (no KV cache, no keys/values); Mamba that of algorithmic design (the scan). (iv) A favorite exam question: "why is the transformer KV cache a *feature* and not just a cost?" — because it stores the history *exactly* (perfect recall), where the SSM state *summarizes* it.
:::

## 6. Efficiency: speculative decoding, quantization {#ch6}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Recap — LLMs module ch. 6
:::

Inference: memory-bound at decoding, KV cache, quantization of weights (INT8/4). Here we demonstrate the two star *test-time* mechanisms: speculative decoding (which buys latency with a small model) and *aware* quantization of activations (GPTQ, AWQ). For costs and green ops: cf. ML Ops module ch. 4 and 10.
::::

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} Y. Leviathan, M. Kalman, Y. Matias, *Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding*, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2211.17192); C. Chen et al., *Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling*, 2023 (arXiv:2302.01318); E. Frantar et al., *GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers*, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2210.17323); J. Lin et al., *AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization*, MLSys 2024 (arXiv:2306.00978).
:::

### 6.1. Speculative decoding: the small proposes, the large disposes

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023)]{.tag} A *draft* model $q$ (small, fast) generates $\gamma$ tokens; the *target* model $p$ (large, slow) *verifies them in a single parallel pass* (the $\gamma$ positions are checked simultaneously — prefilling); each accepted token is free, the first rejected one is corrected by a residual sample; **the distribution of $p$ is preserved exactly** (the paper proves it: correction by sampling according to $\mathrm{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$ at the rejection point). Typical ×2-3 speedups at *identical* quality.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Expected number of tokens per iteration]{.tag} If $\alpha$ is the (average) probability that a token of $q$ is accepted by $p$, the expected number of tokens generated per full iteration (verification + correction) is $$\mathbb{E}[\#\text{tokens}] \;=\; \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma + 1}}{1 - \alpha}.$$ With $\alpha = 0.8$ and $\gamma = 4$: ≈ 3.36 tokens per target pass instead of 1.
:::

::: proof
Let $A$ be the number of tokens accepted before the first rejection. The acceptance of each token is modeled as independent with probability $\alpha$; then $A \sim \mathrm{Geo}(\alpha)$ truncated at $\gamma$: in case of rejection at position $j < \gamma$, the iteration produces $j$ tokens accepted *plus* the corrected token, i.e. $j+1$ tokens; if all $\gamma$ are accepted, the pass produces $\gamma$ tokens *plus* one bonus token sampled from $p$ (position $\gamma{+}1$ is directly generated by the target in the same pass): $j+1$ tokens for all $j \leq \gamma$. Hence $$
\mathbb{E} = \\sum_{j=0}^{\\gamma-1} (1-\\alpha)\,\\alpha^{j}\,(j+1) \\;+\\; \\alpha^{\\gamma}\,(\\gamma + 1).
$$ We recognize the truncated series of the geometric expectation: by using $\sum_{j=0}^{m} \alpha^j = \frac{1-\alpha^{m+1}}{1-\alpha}$ and its derivative for the $(j+1)$ factor, the sum reduces exactly to $\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Critical analysis]{.tag} The gain depends on three clocks: $\alpha$ (small/large agreement — high on ordinary text, low on tricky code or creative outputs); the cost ratio $c$ (verifying $\gamma$ tokens costs more than one decoding step — prefilling); $\gamma$ (too large = many rejections at the last rank). Leviathan et al. give the optimal $\gamma$ as a function of $(\alpha, c)$ — a lab exercise. Descendants: *self-speculation* (the model verifies itself via skipped layers), multiple heads (Medusa), trees — to be documented in your tech watch.
:::

### 6.2. Quantization: GPTQ and AWQ

::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023): layer by layer, Hessian in hand]{.tag} Quantize $W$ into $\hat W$ (e.g. 4 bits, with an error $\Delta = W - \hat W$) by minimizing the error *on the outputs actually produced*: $$\min_{\hat W}\; \bigl\| W X - \hat W X \bigr\|_F^2 \;=\; \min_{\Delta}\; \mathrm{tr}\bigl(\Delta\, X X^\top\, \Delta^\top\bigr), \qquad H = 2 X X^\top,$$ where $X$ is a sample of calibration activations. The algorithm proceeds column by column (greedy): quantize a block of weights, compute the error on the outputs, *propagate it* onto the remaining columns via the Cholesky inverse of $H$ — an approximation of the exact method (OBS/OBD, cf. ML module ch. regularization) made GPU-friendly. Models with billions of parameters are quantized to \~4 bits in a few GPU-hours, with low perplexity losses.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — AWQ (Lin et al., 2024): protecting the salient channels]{.tag} Observation: \~1% of activation channels (per matrix) carry extreme amplitudes; quantizing them naively destroys performance. AWQ *does not quantify them specially* — it **rescales**: multiplying an input channel by $s$ and dividing the weight column by $s$ preserves the exact mathematics of the layer while moving the quantization error *away from* the salient channels (the optimal scale is estimated by search over the calibration activations, without backpropagation). Result: robust 4 bits, no exotic per-group hybrid reconstruction, commodity deployment.
:::

  Method                   Idea                             Cost/advantage                         Limitation
  ------------------------ -------------------------------- -------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------
  Speculative              small proposes, large verifies   ×2-3 latency, exact distribution       needs a good draft; gain varies by domain
  GPTQ                     Hessian-guided quantization      \~4 bits, a few hours of calibration   long-context degradation; tune the groups
  AWQ                      scaling of salient channels      robust 4 bits, no backprop             same low-end limits (3 bits and below)
  (recap) Prefix caching   shared KV                        nearly free prefilling                 prefixes actually shared (ML Ops ch. 4)

::: note
[Critical analysis]{.tag} Perplexity is a poor downstream proxy: a 4-bit model nearly identical in PPL can lose points on long reasoning or safety (learned refusals are subtle — cf. Security module ch. 6); always re-evaluate after quantization on the golden set (ML Ops module ch. 2). Energy: quantization is the #2 green ops lever (ML Ops ch. 10), after functional sobriety.
:::

## 7. LLMs × graphs: the LLGA crossroads {#ch7}

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} H. Wang et al., *Can Language Models Solve Graph Problems in Natural Language?* (NLGraph), NeurIPS 2023 spotlight (arXiv:2305.10037); B. Fatemi, J. Halcrow, B. Perozzi, *Talk like a Graph: Encoding Graphs for Large Language Models*, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.04560); X. He et al., *G-Retriever: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Textual Graph Understanding and Question Answering*, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2402.07630); S. Pan et al., *Unifying Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs: A Roadmap*, IEEE TKDE 2024 (arXiv:2306.08302); survey: W. Chen et al., *Large Language Models on Graphs: A Comprehensive Survey*, 2023 (arXiv:2312.02783).
:::

### 7.1. The "bare" LLM facing serialized graphs

::: ex
[Pivotal result — NLGraph (Wang et al., 2023)]{.tag} 29,370 problems in natural language covering 8 tasks (connectivity, shortest path, maximum independent set… up to the Hamiltonian path and max flow), increasing difficulty (graph size, number of steps). GPT-3/GPT-4 clearly beat chance on the *easy* tasks… and collapse on the hard ones; the authors propose **Build-a-Graph** (making the graph explicit in the prompt) and a **graph translator** (converting the output into structure), which help — without closing the gap with a few-line algorithms. Measured conclusion: LLMs have a preliminary graphical *intuition*, not an algorithmic skill.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 7.1 — Encoding is a first-order variable (Fatemi et al., 2024)]{.tag} "Talk like a Graph" systematically studies *how* to serialize a graph: edge lists, matrix, incident relations, degree-based ordering, etc. Findings: (i) the encoding choice shifts accuracy by tens of points — more than the model choice in some regimes; (ii) the *degree-based* order helps overall; (iii) performance decays with graph size far faster than with text length — it is the *structure*, not the length, that costs. Practical takeaway: serializing a graph is an engineering design act (and of research), not a formality.
:::

### 7.2. Hybridizing: GNN-encoder + LLM-decoder

::: def
[Definition 7.2 — G-Retriever (He et al., NeurIPS 2024)]{.tag} To answer questions over a *large* textual graph (scenes, knowledge maps): (1) retrieve the **relevant subgraph** by formulating retrieval as a **prize-collecting Steiner tree** (PCST — "relevant" nodes carry prizes, edges carry costs: maximize prize − cost of the connected subtree); (2) encode the subgraph with a **GNN** (message passing — Graph ML module ch. 5); (3) inject node embeddings as *soft tokens* into the LLM (learned adapter); (4) joint fine-tuning. Reported effects: better answers and **reduced hallucinations** on ExplaGraphs/SceneGraphs/WebQSP, scalable to graphs of hundreds of thousands of nodes (one never sends the whole graph in the prompt).
:::

### 7.3. Map of the field (the "roadmap")

  Paradigm           Who does what                                Examples
  ------------------ -------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------
  LLM-centric        the LLM reasons; the graph is serialized     NLGraph, Talk like a Graph
  GNN-centric        the GNN encodes; the LLM reads soft tokens   G-Retriever, GNN-as-encoder
  KG-enhanced LLM    the graph feeds the prompt/retrieval         GraphRAG (ch. 3), retrieval over KGs
  LLM-augmented KG   the LLM builds/completes the graph           entity extraction, KG completion
  Systems            hybrid industrial pipelines                  Microsoft GraphRAG (ML Ops module ch. 6)

::: note
[Critical analysis — the LLGA session par excellence]{.tag} (i) *Benchmarks*: NLGraph and friends are small and synthetic; real "enterprise graphs" are noisy, attributed, dynamic — the gulf is wide. (ii) *Prompt cost*: serializing $G=(V,E)$ costs $\mathcal{O}(\|V\| + \|E\|)$ tokens — a modest 10^5^-edge graph saturates any window (ch. 2): compression (summaries, subgraphs, PCST) is not optional. (iii) *Circular evaluation*: judging graph answers with an LLM-judge (ch. 9) — is an LLM fit to judge what it can barely do? (iv) *Open LLGA question*: what share of the "LLM × graph" tasks will reduce to long context + good data (ch. 2-3), and what share will require a real structural component (a GNN)? This is *the* research question of the master — each of your P3/M2 projects can contribute to it.
:::

```python
# Same task, three encodings: the "talk like a graph" experiment in 10 lines
def enc_edges(G):     return "\n".join(f"{u} -- {v}" for u, v in G.edges())
def enc_degree(G):    # edges sorted by decreasing endpoint degree
    d = dict(G.degree())
    es = sorted(G.edges(), key=lambda e: -(d[e[0]] + d[e[1]]))
    return "\n".join(f"{u} -- {v}" for u, v in es)
def enc_incident(G):
    return "\n".join(f"{u} : " + ", ".join(map(str, G[u])) for u in G)

for enc in (enc_edges, enc_degree, enc_incident):
    acc = run_gpt(enc(G), task="connectivite", n=100)
    print(f"{enc.__name__:14s} acc={acc:.2f}  tokens~{len(enc(G))//4}")
```

## 8. Agents: planning, tools, multi-agents {#ch8}

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} S. Yao et al., *ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models*, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2210.03629); T. Schick et al., *Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools*, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2302.04761); N. Shinn et al., *Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning*, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2303.11366); Q. Wu et al., *AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation*, 2023 (arXiv:2308.08155); G. Li et al., *CAMEL: Communicative Agents for Mind Exploration*, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2303.17760).
:::

### 8.1. ReAct: reasoning *and* acting

The ReAct prompt alternates **reasoning traces** (*Thought*) and **actions** (*Action / Observation*) within a single trajectory: the model unrolls "thought → action → observation → thought → …". On HotpotQA and ALFWorld, ReAct beats pure chain-of-thought (fewer hallucinations of impossible steps — the world answers) and pure acting (the observations are *interpreted*). It becomes the default grammar of agents — that of the native "function calls" of current LLMs. RL link ch. 7: ReAct is a *policy* over an interaction tree; the chain-of-thought, its narrative value function.

### 8.2. Toolformer: learning *where* to call the tools

::: prop
[Proposition 8.1 — Toolformer's self-training criterion]{.tag} For each candidate position $t$, insert an API call annotated $c(t)$ (the call *and* its result); compare the next-token prediction loss *without* the call vs *with* its result provided: $$I_t \;=\; -\log p_\theta\bigl(x_t \mid x_{<t}\bigr) \;+\; \log p_\theta\bigl(x_t \mid x_{<t}, c(t)\bigr),$$ (schematic form): $I_t > 0$ — the call *reduces* the loss — flags a *useful* call. The model itself filters its own retained calls, trains on them, and learns to decide *when* to compute (calculator, retrieval, translation, calendar…) — the direct precursor of the native tool-calls of current LLMs (LLMs module ch. 8).
:::

### 8.3. Reflection, multi-agent, and the question of emergence

-   **Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023)**: after a failure, a *verbal feedback* (self-generated or from the environment) is stored and re-injected at the next attempt — "verbal RL": improvement happens in the context, not in the weights. Striking gains on HumanEval and ALFWorld at zero training cost.
-   **CAMEL (Li et al., 2023)**: two agents role-play (user/assistant) to generate instruction *data* — the multi-agent conversation as a data synthesis engine.
-   **AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023)**: a framework where configurable agents (LLM, human, tool) converse programmatically — the industrial design pattern of multi-agent teams (orchestrator, critics, executors), to be connected to the guardrails and the tracing of the module ML Ops ch. 8.

::: prop
[Proposition 8.2 — The unforgiving arithmetic of chains]{.tag} A $k$-step task with per-step success $p$ succeeds with $p^k$ (independence): $p = 0.98$, $k = 50$ → 36%. For a reliable agent, three levers: shorten the chains (composite tools), make each step reliable (Reflexion, retries, deterministic tools), and *avoid long chains where an algorithm exists* — an agent that plans a topological sort step by step is an architecture mistake (ch. 7: NLGraph).
:::

::: note
[Critical analysis]{.tag} (i) *Evaluation*: agent gains are measured on environments (ALFWorld, HumanEval, SWE-bench-like) whose fidelity to the real world is debated — unmodeled costs (ML Ops ch. 4/8), noisy environment, absent adversary. (ii) *Multi-agent emergence*: when "several agents" beat "one agent", is it emergence — or the effect of a better prompt / more compute? Several ablation studies suggest the second reading: demand honest ablations (a single agent, same token budget). (iii) *Safety*: every tool is an injection surface (Security module ch. 5-6); multi-agent environments multiply implicit trusts — the least-privilege pattern (ML Ops ch. 8-9) remains the only serious defense. (iv) *RL link*: the LLM agent as a policy — agentic "behaviors" are now trained by RLVR on trajectories (ch. 1): the prompt/training boundary is shifting under our eyes.
:::

## 9. Evaluation: contamination, judge bias {#ch9}

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} C. Xu, S. Guan, D. Greene, M.-T. Kechadi, *Benchmark Data Contamination of Large Language Models: A Survey*, 2024 (arXiv:2406.04244); L. Zheng et al., *Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena*, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2306.05685); P. Wang et al., *Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators*, ACL 2024 (arXiv:2305.17926); P. Liang et al., *Holistic Evaluation of Language Models* (HELM), TMLR 2023 (arXiv:2211.09110).
:::

### 9.1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Benchmark data contamination (BDC)]{.tag} The pollution of a benchmark when its data (questions *and/or* answers) have been seen during pre-training — accidental (the web contains the solutions), or even deliberate (training *on* the test's variant). Signals: n-gram overlaps with the corpus, embedding similarity, abnormally low test perplexity, the ability to complete the items without their instruction, "random" performance on renamed variants (changing the figures of a math problem). Responses: canaries ("do not train on this string"), *dynamic* benchmarks refreshed (e.g. LiveBench), private sets, kept-current evaluations (challenges with a cutoff date).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.2 — What a contaminated score estimates (and what it does not)]{.tag} A benchmark measures performance on a task distribution $P_{\text{test}}$. If the model has seen $n$ examples of $P_{\text{test}}$ during training, the score observes a mixture $\rho \cdot \text{memory} + (1-\rho) \cdot \text{generalization}$: the estimand has shifted — the score overestimates *and* distorts comparisons (the models trained more recently, on larger corpora, are more contaminated: the bias advances with time). The methodological remedy: report jointly (i) the raw score, (ii) the score on re-generated variants, (iii) an overlap measure — and treat the (i)-(ii) gap as an interval, not as noise.
:::

### 9.2. LLM judges: useful, biased, calibratable

MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023) validates the LLM judge: agreement with human preferences is high (GPT-4 as judge ≈ 80%+ of inter-human agreement level), which legitimizes its industrial use (ML Ops module ch. 5). But the biases are systematic: **position** (favoring the first answer — corrected by alternating order), **verbosity** (long answers win), **self-preference** (the judge favors the answers of its own model family). Wang et al. (ACL 2024) show that a simple order swap flips a substantial share of verdicts — "not fair evaluators". HELM (Liang et al.) answers with the *holistic*: same models, dozens of scenarios, multiple metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, bias, toxicity…), published protocol — evaluation as a slow science versus the leaderboard as a fast sport.

::: note
[Critical analysis — the "methods" session]{.tag} (i) *Goodhart*: every public benchmark becomes a training objective — the value of a score decays with its popularity; (ii) *Variance*: a leaderboard at ±0.5 points with 500 questions ranks nothing (cf. ML Ops module ch. 2, Hoeffding); (iii) *Judge the judge*: calibrate each judge on a human golden set *before* using it (measured biases, alternating orders, rubrics); (iv) *Saturation*: when everyone exceeds 90% accuracy, the benchmark measures noise — move to the dynamic/adversarial evaluations (red teaming of the Security module ch. 10, agents of ch. 8). LLGA rule: **no evaluation number without its protocol** — neither in the papers you read, nor in your own.
:::

```python
# N-gram contamination detection (sketch, thresholds to calibrate)
def ngrams(s, n=13):  return {" ".join(s.split()[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(s.split())-n+1)}

def overlap(test_item, pretrain_index):     # pretrain_index: set of shingles
    q = ngrams(test_item.question) | ngrams(test_item.answer)
    return len(q & pretrain_index) / max(len(q), 1)

# measurement: overlap distribution per benchmark -- a non-negligible mass
# above 0.8 on "public" items (GSM8K-like) = contamination signal
```

## 10. Open problems {#ch10}

::: ex
[Today's readings]{.tag} P. Villalobos, J. Sevilla, L. Heim, et al., *Will we run out of data? Limits of LLM scaling based on human-generated data*, 2022 (arXiv:2211.04325); I. Shumailov et al., *AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data* (the "curse of recursion"), Nature 2024; H. Yu et al., *Continual Learning of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey*, 2024 (arXiv:2402.01344).
:::

### 10.1. Data exhaustion

::: prop
[Proposition 10.1 — The Villalobos et al. (2022) window]{.tag} The stock of "quality" public text produced by humans is finite (on the order of a few 10^14^ tokens actually usable); training set sizes grow exponentially (\~2 to 2.5×/year at the time of the study); by extrapolating the two curves, **the effective stock would be exhausted between 2026 and 2032** — high-quality data first. This is not a prediction of progress stopping but a regime change: the constraint shifts to the data side.
:::

The answers in progress: **synthetic data** (models generate their own training material — with the risk of **model collapse**: Shumailov et al. show, on toy models and Gaussians, that recursive training on generated data erodes the distribution tails — diversity collapses generation after generation); **data efficiency** (tokens counted, curriculum, "quality over quantity"); new sources (audio, video, interactions); **rights** — the question becomes legal (AI Act: copyright policy of GPAI — Security module ch. 10) before being purely technical.

### 10.2. Continual learning

LLMs are *frozen* at publication: any change requires a new training run or a fine-tune (with its train: catastrophic forgetting of earlier capabilities, safety regression — ML Ops module ch. 2 and 7). *Continual learning* targets incremental updating: replay of a core of experiences, regularization toward the previous weights, additive modules (successive LoRAs, merging), *model merging* (combining the weights of specialists — simple averages, TIES: surprising and under-theorized results). The Yu et al. (2024) survey maps the field; the honest assessment: no scheme dominates yet, and the success criterion itself is blurry (remember *what*, from how many versions back?).

### 10.3. Other fronts — and conclusion of the seminar

-   **Memory vs context vs weights** (ch. 2-3): where should knowledge be stored — parameters, KV, external index? The marginal cost of each byte differs by three orders of magnitude; the answer will depend on serving economics (ML Ops module ch. 3-4);
-   **Reasoning beyond the verifiable** (ch. 1): extending reliable rewards beyond math/code;
-   **Safety at scale**: statistical alignment facing competing objectives (Security module ch. 5-6);
-   **Interpretability as a science**: from IRM (probes, SAE) to verifiable mechanics (Security module ch. 1-3);
-   **LLGA**: the LLM × graphs confrontation (ch. 7) remains an open construction site — serialization, GNN-LLM hybrids, incremental GraphRAG: *your* internship topics.

::: note
[Module conclusion]{.tag} The seminar had you read ten families of papers with a single grid: claim, evidence, costs, reproducibility, LLGA link. This is the skill the master wants to install: quickly read the essentials, doubt methodically, and connect every advance to the complete system (data → training → serving → evaluation → safety) described by the LLMs, ML Ops and Explainability/Security/Privacy modules. The instructors of this proposed course are not confirmed; the cited papers and standards form the foundation, and the LLGA (LLMs & Graphs) group of the X will provide the guest sessions when relevant.
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **Reading notes (running thread).** One sheet per session (claim / evidence / costs / reproducibility / LLGA link) on the pivotal paper; two sheets graded in depth: DeepSeek-R1 (ch. 1) and G-Retriever (ch. 7).
2.  **Self-consistency (ch. 1).** On a GSM8K sample: greedy vs self-consistency (k = 5, 20); plot accuracy vs k and accuracy vs cost (tokens); check that voting on the *final answer extracted* beats voting on the raw chain — why?
3.  **Toy RLVR (ch. 1).** Implement a mini-GRPO (cf. LLMs module ch. 5) with a binary format reward on a small model; observe the lengthening of the generations — a domestic "aha moment"; discuss reward hacking (does the model cheat the format?).
4.  **RoPE and extension (ch. 2).** Numerically verify prop. 2.2 (dot products invariant under translation); extend a small model 512 → 2048 by interpolation then by YaRN; compare perplexity and a recall task (needle) before/after.
5.  **Simulated ring attention (ch. 2).** Implement blockwise attention with ring passing over 4 simulated "GPUs" (processes); verify exactness vs dense attention; measure communication vs compute (overlap).
6.  **Agent memory (ch. 3).** Build a memory stream with the recency/importance/relevance triptych (prop. 3.1); add the reflection loop; test on 20 simulated sessions; ablation of each component of the score.
7.  **MoE routing (ch. 4).** Load Mixtral (open weights) and instrument the router; measure the load distribution per expert over 3 corpora (code, math, prose); reproduce the specialization figure — and its variability; implement the auxiliary loss of Switch on a toy MoE and show the balancing.
8.  **SSM scan (ch. 5).** Implement the SSM recurrence then the prefix scan (prop. 5.2 for the LTI case; selective version for Mamba); compare the GPU memory of the three modes (recurrence / FFT convolution / scan) on L = 8k; test the exact recall of a distant association — transformer vs SSM (the ch. 5 critique).
9.  **Speculative decoding (ch. 6).** Code the draft/verify scheme with residual re-sampling; verify empirically thm. 6.2 (count the tokens/iteration for measured $\alpha$); find the optimal $\gamma$ for $(\alpha, c)$ measured on your machine.
10. **Graph encodings (ch. 7).** Reproduce "Talk like a Graph" on 3 NLGraph tasks × 4 encodings (code from ch. 7); test the hypothesis "it is the structure, not the length" by matching lengths; a light G-Retriever: replace the PCST with a weighted shortest path and compare.
11. **Agents (ch. 8).** A ReAct agent with 3 tools, one of them unreliable (bad output); measure per-step $p$ and the $p^k$ law (prop. 8.2); add Reflexion and measure gain vs cost; multi-agent ablation: 2 "specialized" agents vs 1 agent with the same token budget.
12. **Contamination (ch. 9).** The ch. 9 n-gram detector on a small corpus; build 20 re-generated variants of a toy benchmark; measure the raw/variant gap for two models — and the judges' asymmetry (alternating order) on MT-Bench-like setups.
13. **Mini-review (ch. 10).** Write a 4-page "position paper": *"In 2030, will knowledge live in the weights, the context or the index?"* — drawing on at least six chapters of the seminar and two modules of the master.
